gaps.text: Combining several spectroscopy methods (data fusion) (Fusion level: keep one model per method as the baseline, then concatenate the two blocks after scaling them to a common intensity range. Both channels must be collected from the same spot and aligned to a common time step, with each instrument keeping its own calibration and diagnostics. The fused model must beat the best single method on held-out samples, otherwise the second channel is not justified.)

items.finding: This review describes low-level data fusion as the simplest way to combine inputs by placing variables from different sources one after another in a new data matrix.
items.how_it_applies: This could inform the baseline concatenation step in O3, where MIR ATR and fluorescence blocks are joined after scaling to a common range.
items.limits_and_transfer_risks: The source is a general PAT review and does not specify biological tissue, MIR ATR or fluorescence, scaling, alignment, or held-out validation.

citation.quote: Low-level data fusion (LLDF) is considered the simplest method to achieve a combination of inputs. In this case, the data is rearranged into a new data matrix, where the variables coming from different sources are placed one after the other.
citation.label: E01 ¶31

items.finding: This review states that before fusing multiple data sources, one should evaluate each dataset's contribution and complementarity.
items.how_it_applies: This could inform the G1 requirement to keep single-method baselines and check whether the second channel adds complementary information before accepting the fused model.
items.limits_and_transfer_risks: The source is a general PAT review and does not specify MIR ATR, fluorescence, biological tissues, scaling, alignment, or a held-out performance criterion.

citation.quote: Before fusing data from multiple sources, it is essential to evaluate the contribution of each dataset to the model and its complementarity.
